notes.meaning: Judas stepped forward to greet Jesus with a kiss, which was the usual sign of love and respect from a disciple. Jesus openly questioned him, asking if he was really using a warm sign of friendship to hand over his Master. The question showed that Jesus knew the wicked plot and saw right through the disguise.

Seeing that the crowd was about to seize Jesus, the disciples asked if they should attack with their swords. They had two weapons ready and felt this was the right moment to defend their Lord. Although their loyalty was sincere, their sudden zeal ran ahead of God's plan.

Before waiting for an answer, one disciple swung his sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant. This was Peter, who tried to strike the man's head but missed his mark. Luke, who was a doctor, carefully recorded that it was the man's right ear.

Jesus stopped the fighting at once, telling his followers to put an end to the violence. He then reached out, touched the servant's bleeding ear, and healed him completely. By doing this, Jesus showed mercy to an enemy and prevented his disciples from being arrested as rebels.

differ.view: Some take Jesus' words as a polite request to his captors to let his hands go so he could heal the wounded servant.
John Calvin viewed the healing as Jesus protecting the gospel from slander, so enemies could not accuse him of leading a violent rebellion.

notes.meaning: Jesus turned to the chief priests, temple guards, and elders who had come to arrest him. He asked why they came with swords and wooden clubs, as if they were tracking down a dangerous bandit. Their heavy weapons showed their own guilty conscience and fear of the crowds.

Jesus reminded them that he had taught out in the open in the temple every day without being touched. They chose the middle of the night instead because this was their permitted time, when the power of darkness held sway. Jesus willingly surrendered because God allowed evil this brief and limited hour.

The officers arrested Jesus and brought him directly into the courtyard of the high priest's palace. Peter followed the crowd, but he stayed far behind so he would not be in danger. He cared enough to follow his Master, yet fear kept him from standing openly with him.

The servants and guards lit a fire in the middle of the open courtyard because of the cold night air. Peter walked over and sat down among them, trying to blend in with the crowd. By sitting among Jesus' enemies, Peter placed himself in a place of great temptation.

A servant girl noticed Peter sitting near the fire and stared closely at his face in the bright light. She told everyone nearby that this man had been with Jesus. The light of the fire made it impossible for Peter to stay hidden in the dark.

Peter immediately rejected her words and said, 'Woman, I do not know him.' Caught off guard by a servant girl's comment, his courage vanished. This was the first of three times Peter failed to stand up for his Lord.

A little later, another person saw Peter and insisted that he was one of Jesus' disciples. Peter denied it flatly, answering, 'Man, I am not.' Having told one lie to protect himself, he found it even easier to tell a second one.

About an hour went by before another man spoke up, firmly declaring that Peter was definitely a follower of Jesus. The man pointed out that Peter was from the region of Galilee, since his accent gave him away. During that whole hour, Peter had remained in the dangerous courtyard instead of turning away.

Peter denied the charge a third time, claiming he had no idea what the man was talking about. Right as he spoke those words, a rooster began to crow in the early morning. Peter had now denied his Lord three times, exactly as Jesus had predicted.

The Lord turned around and looked directly at Peter at the very moment the rooster crowed. Peter suddenly remembered Jesus warning him that he would deny him three times before the rooster crowed that day. That look was filled with sorrow and mercy, and it touched Peter's heart with grace to bring him to repentance.

Peter rushed out of the courtyard and cried bitterly in deep grief over his failure. His tears showed genuine repentance, because he hated his sin and remembered his Lord's love. Unlike Judas, who fell into despair and killed himself, Peter's sorrow led him back to God.

The guards holding Jesus began to make fun of him and beat him. They treated him with cruel abuse through the night without giving him any rest before his trial. Jesus patiently suffered the shame and blows that sinners deserved to receive.

The men covered Jesus' eyes with a cloth and slapped him in the face, demanding that he prophesy who struck him. They mocked his reputation as a prophet who knew hidden things. Ironically, Jesus had just accurately foretold Peter's denials at that very hour.

The guards continued to shout many other insulting and wicked words against Jesus. The leaders later claimed Jesus was guilty of blasphemy, but Luke shows that these abusive men were the ones truly blaspheming God's Son. Jesus bore all their harsh words without striking back.

As soon as the sun rose, the council of Jewish elders, chief priests, and scribes met together and brought Jesus before them. Jewish law required trials for life and death to take place in the daylight, so they gathered early to make their decision seem lawful. They were eager to finish condemning him as quickly as they could.

The council demanded that Jesus tell them plainly if he was the Christ, God's chosen King. Jesus replied that even if he told them, they would never believe him. They were not seeking the truth, because they had already decided in their hearts to destroy him.

Jesus told them that if he asked them a question to defend his claim, they would refuse to answer him or let him go free. He had previously asked them questions in the temple that left them silent and unwilling to admit the truth. They were unfair judges who cared nothing for justice.

Jesus announced that from now on, the Son of Man would sit at the right hand of God's mighty power. He pointed to the Old Testament promises of an exalted ruler in heaven. Even though he stood there as a prisoner on trial, he would soon reign in glory as the true Judge of all people.

The leaders immediately asked if he was claiming to be the Son of God, and Jesus replied, 'You say that I am.' His words were a clear Jewish way of saying yes. He openly declared who he was, knowing that this truthful answer would cost him his life.

The council members declared that they had no need for any other witnesses, since they had heard his confession with their own ears. They treated his claim of divine sonship as worthy of death for blasphemy. Instead of testing whether his words were true, they rushed ahead to seal his condemnation.
